title: Saudi Arabia | SAMA AML/CTF Compliance and Targeted Financial Sanctions
tagline: Saudi AML and CTF Laws, SAMA's AML/CTF Guide and the 2025 sanctions rules in practice: CDD, FIU reporting, freezing and your bank's programme.
sectors: Conventional banks licensed and supervised by SAMA
description:
A country-specific quest for staff of **conventional banks supervised by the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA)**. It is built on the **Anti-Money Laundering Law (Royal Decree M/20, 2017)** and its Implementing Regulation, the **Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing (Royal Decree M/21)** and its Implementing Regulations, **SAMA's AML/CTF Guide (2019)**, SAMA's **Account Opening Rules**, the **Rules for the Implementation of Targeted Financial Sanctions (December 2025)** and SAMA's **Guidance on Assessing Business Risks related to ML, TF and Proliferation Financing (December 2025)**, with reporting to the **General Directorate of Financial Intelligence (Saudi FIU)**.

Article 14/1(e) of the AML Implementing Regulation and Article 18 of the CTF Implementing Regulations require ongoing employee training, and Section 11 of SAMA's Guide expects every employee to be trained before starting work, refreshed regularly and tested at least once a year. This quest is therefore for everyone from tellers to board members. You will learn the offences, the risk-based approach, CDD, beneficial ownership and PEP rules, how to escalate and report without tipping off, ten-year record keeping, sanctions screening and freezing, proliferation financing risk, the compliance and audit functions, and the penalties SAMA and the courts can impose.

This quest builds knowledge of the Saudi framework; it does not replace your bank's own AML/CTF and sanctions policies and procedures, which you must always follow.
audience: All employees of SAMA-supervised conventional banks who need AML/CTF induction or annual refresher training
Tellers, customer service and call-centre staff who must complete KYC and AML/CFT training before taking up their roles
Onboarding, KYC, transaction monitoring and sanctions screening teams who apply CDD, EDD and TFS controls
Payments, remittance and trade staff exposed to wire transfer, sanctions evasion and proliferation financing risks
Compliance officers, internal auditors, senior managers and board members accountable for the AML/CTF programme
outcomes: Explain the Saudi AML/CTF framework, the money laundering and terrorist financing offences and the roles of SAMA, the Saudi FIU and the permanent committees
Apply the risk-based approach to CDD, beneficial ownership, simplified and enhanced measures and PEPs under the AML Implementing Regulation and SAMA's Guide
Escalate and report suspicious transactions to the Saudi FIU, avoid tipping off and keep records for at least ten years
Screen, handle alerts, freeze without delay and notify SAMA under the December 2025 Targeted Financial Sanctions Rules
Describe the business risk assessment, the compliance and audit functions, SAMA's training rules and the supervisory and criminal penalties

quest.name: Guardians of the Oasis
quest.premise: You have just joined the Financial Crime Compliance team of Wahat Bank, a fictional conventional bank supervised by SAMA, with its head office in Riyadh and branches in Jeddah and Dammam. SAMA has announced a review of AML/CTF and sanctions controls, and its new December 2025 sanctions rules and business risk guidance are in force. With compliance head Noura Al-Qahtani, branch manager Faisal Al-Harbi, sanctions specialist Arjun Menon and customer service officer Sara Al-Dossary, clear five stages, then face the final boss: briefing chief executive Majed Al-Shehri before SAMA arrives.

badge.name: Saudi AML Guardian
badge.description: Awarded to bank staff who can apply Saudi AML/CTF law and SAMA's rules: know the customer, report right, freeze fast and run a sound programme.

cast.name: Noura Al-Qahtani
cast.role: Head of AML/CTF Compliance, your mentor

sessions.title: The Saudi Framework: Laws, Offences and Who Does What
sessions.summary: Map the Saudi AML/CTF framework: the 2017 Anti-Money Laundering Law, the Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing Law, their implementing regulations, SAMA's AML/CTF Guide and the 2025 sanctions and risk instruments, the authorities involved, the two offences and your own training duty.
objectives: Name the laws, implementing regulations and SAMA instruments that make up the Saudi AML/CTF framework for banks
Describe the roles of SAMA, the Saudi FIU, the permanent committees and the Public Prosecution
Explain the money laundering offence under Article 2 of the AML Law and the terrorist financing offence under Article 47 of the CTF Law
Explain why every bank employee must be trained before starting work and tested at least once a year

cards.title: Day one at Wahat Bank
cards.setting: AML/CTF Compliance floor, Wahat Bank head office, King Fahd Road, Riyadh. 8:30 am.

lines.text: Your new badge says Wahat Bank, Financial Crime Compliance. Before you reach your desk, a message pops up: 'Meeting room 4. Now. Noura.'
Welcome! I'm Noura Al-Qahtani, head of AML/CTF compliance. You picked a lively month to join us.
SAMA has announced a thematic review of AML/CTF and targeted financial sanctions controls across banks, and the new sanctions rules from December 2025 are on the list.
(on screen from Jeddah) Faisal here, Al-Hamra branch. My new tellers ask why they sat an AML course before they were even allowed near a counter.
And my screening team keeps asking which rule is a law, which is a regulation and which is a SAMA instruction. It matters when we write procedures.
Both fair questions. Today we climb the Rulebook Gate: the laws, the authorities, the two offences and why training comes first.
By the end of this stage you will be able to answer Faisal's tellers yourself. Ready?

cards.title: The Saudi framework in six scenes

scenes.heading: The AML Law
scenes.narration: The Anti-Money Laundering Law, issued by Royal Decree M/20 in 2017, defines the offence, sets the preventive duties of financial institutions and creates the penalties. It replaced the earlier 2012 law.

scenes.heading: The CTF Law
scenes.narration: The Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing, issued by Royal Decree M/21 in the same year, does the same for terrorist financing, with its own reporting and tipping-off articles.

scenes.heading: Implementing regulations
scenes.narration: Each law has an implementing regulation that adds detail. For example, Article 14/1 of the AML regulation lists what a bank's internal controls must contain, including ongoing employee training.

scenes.heading: SAMA's instruments
scenes.narration: SAMA supervises banks and publishes its instructions in the SAMA Rulebook: the 2019 AML/CTF Guide, the Account Opening Rules, and two new texts from December 2025 on targeted sanctions and on business risk assessment.

scenes.heading: Where reports go
scenes.narration: Suspicious transaction reports go to the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence, the Saudi FIU, which works under the oversight of the President of State Security with operational independence.

scenes.heading: Your bank's policies
scenes.narration: Wahat Bank turns all of this into policies approved by senior management. Those policies bind every employee, from the board to the newest teller.

cards.title: Layers of the Saudi AML/CTF framework
cards.caption: Each layer must fit the one above it. Your daily procedures sit at the bottom and must respect every layer.

items.label: AML Law and CTF Law
items.detail: Royal Decrees M/20 and M/21 of 2017: offences, preventive duties, FIU, supervision and penalties.

items.label: Implementing regulations
items.detail: Detail on risk assessment, CDD, PEPs, reporting, internal controls and training.

items.label: SAMA AML/CTF Guide
items.detail: Circular of November 2019: how SAMA expects banks to meet the legal duties, section by section.

items.label: SAMA rules and guidance
items.detail: Account Opening Rules, TFS Rules (Dec 2025), business risk guidance (Dec 2025).

items.label: Wahat Bank policies
items.detail: Approved by senior management, applied to all branches and majority-owned subsidiaries.

cards.title: Who does what in Saudi Arabia?
cards.prompt: Match each authority to its role in the AML/CTF system.

pairs.right: Supervises banks for AML/CTF, inspects them, issues instructions and can impose measures and fines

pairs.left: Saudi FIU (General Directorate of Financial Intelligence)
pairs.right: Receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports and shares results with competent authorities
Can identify high-risk countries and set countermeasures that banks must apply (Article 11)
Handles UN counter-terrorism sanctions mechanisms under the Presidency of State Security
Investigates and prosecutes ML and TF crimes and can order records, searches and provisional seizure

cards.question: A Wahat Bank analyst decides a customer's transfers are suspicious. Under Article 15 of the AML Law, who receives the report?
options: SAMA's banking supervision department
The General Directorate of Financial Intelligence (the Saudi FIU)
The Public Prosecution office nearest the branch
The Anti-Money Laundering Permanent Committee
cards.explanation: Article 15 requires suspicious transactions to be reported promptly and directly to the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence. SAMA supervises the bank but is not the recipient of suspicious transaction reports, and the Public Prosecution acts later, on the FIU's dissemination.

cards.title: Money laundering under Article 2
cards.body:
The AML Law treats four kinds of conduct as money laundering when the person **knows** the funds are proceeds of crime:

- **Converting or transferring** them, or carrying out any transaction on them, to disguise their origin or help an offender escape the consequences.
- **Acquiring, possessing or using** them.
- **Concealing or disguising** their nature, source, movement, ownership or location.
- **Attempting, assisting, abetting, advising or facilitating** any of the above.

Three further points matter for bankers:

- **Separate offence (Article 4):** no conviction for the predicate crime is needed, wherever it happened.
- **Intent can be inferred** from objective facts, so 'I did not ask' is no defence when the circumstances were obvious.
- **Legal persons are liable (Article 3)**, and that does not shield board members, managers or employees who acted for the bank.

cards.title: Is this money laundering under Article 2?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each act, done knowingly with criminal proceeds, falls within Article 2 of the AML Law.
buckets: Not money laundering on these facts

items.text: Splitting fraud proceeds across relatives' accounts to hide who owns them
Buying a car with money the buyer knows came from drug dealing
A friend advising a fraudster how to route funds through a trading company
Trying to deposit bribe money that the bank refuses to accept
Depositing a documented end-of-service payment from a known employer
Receiving a salary transfer that matches the customer's employment contract
Moving smuggling proceeds abroad to put them out of investigators' reach
Paying a supplier invoice that matches goods actually delivered

cards.title: The donation question
cards.setting: Video call between Riyadh and Jeddah, 11:15 am.

lines.text: Here is one from my branch. A customer collects cash donations from colleagues every month and sends them abroad. The money is clean salary money. That can't be terrorist financing, can it?
Under Article 47 of the CTF Law it can. The source of the money does not matter: legitimate or illegitimate, it is caught if it is meant for a terrorist act, a terrorist or a terrorist entity.
And it doesn't need the attack to happen, or even the money to be spent?
Correct. The offence is complete even if the crime never takes place or the funds are never used. That is why we look at purpose and destination, not just origin.
So my tellers need to think about where money is going, not only where it came from.
Exactly. Let's test that instinct.

cards.title: Clean money, troubling destination
cards.situation: Hamad, a long-standing customer at Faisal's branch, deposits about SAR 18,000 in cash each month and transfers it to a newly opened account abroad in the name of a charity nobody at the branch has heard of. He says his colleagues contributed from their salaries. When the teller asks about the charity's work, Hamad becomes vague and says the organisers 'prefer not to publicise'.

choices.text: Process it: the money comes from salaries, so there is no criminal source to worry about
choices.outcome: This misreads the CTF Law. Article 47 covers funds from legitimate sources too, so a clean origin does not settle the question. Ignoring the destination could leave the bank facilitating terrorist financing.

choices.text: Refuse the transfer and tell Hamad the bank suspects his charity of funding terrorism
choices.outcome: Refusing may be right, but telling him about the suspicion breaches the tipping-off ban in Article 71 of the CTF Law and could damage an investigation.

choices.text: Complete the transaction steps the policy allows, record the facts and escalate internally to the AML/CTF unit without saying anything to Hamad
choices.outcome: Best choice. The unusual destination and vague answers are grounds for an internal report. The AML/CTF unit can screen the recipient, assess the case and, if suspicion is confirmed, report promptly to the FIU.

choices.text: Ask Hamad to bring a letter from the charity next month and decide then
choices.outcome: Waiting a month while transfers continue delays a report that may be needed now. Gathering information is useful, but escalation should not wait.

cards.title: Two offences side by side
cards.caption: The preventive duties are almost identical in both laws; the offences differ in what they look at.

items.label: What it targets
items.right: Funds for terrorist acts, terrorists or entities

items.label: Needs an outcome?
items.right: No attack or use of funds needed

cards.title: Key terms in the Saudi laws

cards.back: Any crime under Saudi law, or an act abroad that is a crime there and would be one in the Kingdom, that generates proceeds.
Funds obtained directly or indirectly from a predicate offence, including funds converted into other assets.
The natural person who ultimately owns or controls a customer, or on whose behalf a transaction is made.
The body that checks compliance with the law; for banks this is SAMA.
A bank licensed in a country where it has no physical presence and no regulated group behind it. Saudi banks may not deal with one.
A temporary ban on moving or using funds, ordered by a court or competent authority.

cards.question: Which statement about the terrorist financing offence in Article 47 of the CTF Law is correct?
options: It applies only if the funds come from a crime
It applies only once a terrorist act has taken place
It can apply to lawfully earned money intended for a terrorist entity
It applies only to transfers sent outside the Kingdom
cards.explanation: Article 47 covers funds from legitimate or illegitimate sources, inside or outside the Kingdom, and applies even if the terrorist crime never occurs or the funds are not used.

cards.title: Why you were trained before your first day
cards.caption: Account Opening Rule 9 adds that tellers and customer service staff may not be assigned before KYC, AML/CFT and ethics courses.

items.label: AML regulation 14/1(e)
items.detail: Internal controls must include ongoing employee training programmes.

items.label: CTF regulations Art. 18(1)(f)
items.detail: CFT policies must include continuing employee training.

items.label: SAMA Guide 11.2(a)
items.detail: Train current staff, and new staff before they start work, then repeat.

items.label: SAMA Guide 11.4
items.detail: Test staff knowledge and training quality at least once a year.

items.label: SAMA Guide 11.5
items.detail: Keep records of training given, attendance and dates.

cards.title: Real case: SAMA suspends an exchange company (2017)
cards.body:
In November 2017 SAMA announced that it had suspended a licensed money exchange company, Saleh Hussain Al-Amoudi Sons, from money changing business until it put its affairs in order and obtained SAMA's approval to restart.

According to SAMA's statement, the company had not complied with SAMA's regulatory and supervisory requirements, including measures communicated to financial institutions under the AML/CTF rules then in force. SAMA said it had already issued **several warnings** asking the company to fix the problems, and that the suspension would stay until full compliance, including with AML/CTF instructions, was proven.

**Lessons for a bank:**

- SAMA treats AML/CTF failures as a licensing matter, not just a paperwork issue.
- Warnings are a stage, not the end: ignoring them escalates the response.
- 'We were going to fix it' is not a defence once the supervisor has asked.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: The framework has layers: the 2017 AML Law and CTF Law, their implementing regulations, SAMA's AML/CTF Guide and newer SAMA rules, then your bank's policies.
SAMA supervises banks; suspicious transaction reports go only to the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence (Saudi FIU).
Money laundering (Article 2) is a separate offence: no predicate conviction is needed and intent can be inferred from the facts.
Terrorist financing (Article 47) covers clean money too, and the offence exists even if no attack happens.
Training is a legal control: before you start work, repeated over time, tested at least annually and recorded.

cards.prompt: Think of the first customer interaction you will have in your role. Which part of the framework you met today would apply to it, and who in your bank would you call if something felt wrong?

quiz.question: Which instrument contains Article 14/1(e), requiring ongoing employee training programmes as part of a bank's AML controls?
options: SAMA's Rules for the Implementation of Targeted Financial Sanctions
The Banking Control Law issued in 1966
The Saudi Central Bank Law
The Implementing Regulation to the Anti-Money Laundering Law
quiz.explanation: Article 14 of the AML Law leaves the content of internal controls to the implementing regulation, and paragraph 14/1(e) lists ongoing employee training. The TFS Rules have their own training chapter, but 14/1(e) is in the AML regulation.

quiz.question: Under Article 4 of the AML Law, what is needed before someone can be convicted of money laundering?
options: Proof that the funds are proceeds of crime, without a predicate conviction
A report from the bank that handled the funds
A confession from the person who committed the predicate crime
A final conviction for the predicate offence in Saudi Arabia
quiz.explanation: Article 4 makes money laundering a separate offence; neither a conviction for the predicate offence nor a bank report is a precondition, and intent may be inferred from objective circumstances.

quiz.question: A teller asks why she had to complete AML/CFT and KYC courses before being posted to the counter. Which SAMA text requires this for tellers and customer service staff?
options: Article 47 of the CTF Law
Rule 9 of SAMA's Account Opening Rules
Article 25 of the AML Law
Section 13 of SAMA's AML/CTF Guide
quiz.explanation: Rule 9 of the Account Opening Rules says banks should not assign tellers or customer service staff until they have attended KYC, AML/CFT and professional ethics courses. Section 13 of the Guide deals with correspondent relationships and Article 25 with supervisory measures.

quiz.question: A customer sends his own salary savings abroad to a group he knows is planning an attack. The attack is later foiled and the money is never spent. Under the CTF Law, what is the position?
options: Only an attempt, because the funds were never used
No offence, because the money was lawfully earned
The terrorist financing offence may still be complete
No offence, because the attack did not take place
quiz.explanation: Article 47 covers funds from legitimate sources and applies even if the crime does not occur or the funds are not used. Lawful origin and a foiled plot do not remove the offence.

quiz.question: What does SAMA's AML/CTF Guide (paragraph 11.4) require regarding staff knowledge?
options: A written examination before each promotion
Testing only for compliance staff and internal auditors
An external certificate renewed every three years
Testing of staff knowledge and training quality, at least annually
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.4 asks institutions to test employees' knowledge of AML/CTF requirements and the quality of training periodically, at least once a year. It is not limited to specialists or tied to promotion.

quiz.question: Wahat Bank is prosecuted for money laundering committed in its name. Which statement reflects Article 3 of the AML Law?
options: The bank's liability does not shield the staff and directors involved
Only the bank can be punished, never its employees
Directors are liable only if SAMA consents
Employees are liable only if they personally gained
quiz.explanation: Article 3 makes a legal person criminally liable while keeping the liability of chairmen, board members, employees and others who acted in its name or for its account.

quiz.question: Who exercises oversight over the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence under Article 17 of the AML Law?
options: The Capital Market Authority
The President of State Security
The Minister of Finance
The Governor of SAMA
quiz.explanation: Article 17 places the Directorate under the oversight of the President of State Security, with adequate operational independence. SAMA is the banks' supervisor, not the FIU's overseer.

quiz.question: A Saudi bank officer receives proceeds of a fraud committed in another country, where fraud is a crime. Can that fraud be a predicate offence under the AML Law?
options: No, only crimes committed inside the Kingdom count
Only if the foreign country has convicted someone
Yes, if it would also be an offence had it been committed in the Kingdom
Only if the funds exceed a set value threshold
quiz.explanation: Article 1 defines a predicate offence to include acts abroad that are crimes where committed and would be offences under Saudi law. No foreign conviction or minimum amount is required.

quiz.question: Which pair of SAMA instruments was issued in December 2025?
options: The Banking Control Law and its implementation rules
The Counter-Fraud Framework and the Cyber Security Framework
The Targeted Financial Sanctions Rules and the business risk assessment guidance
The AML/CTF Guide and the Account Opening Rules
quiz.explanation: SAMA issued the Rules for the Implementation of Targeted Financial Sanctions on 7 December 2025 and the Guidance on Assessing Business Risks related to ML, TF and PF on 31 December 2025. The AML/CTF Guide dates from 2019.

quiz.question: A relationship manager says: 'I only processed the transfers; I never knew the money was dirty.' The circumstances made the criminal origin obvious. Why may that not help him?
options: Bank staff are liable without any knowledge at all
Knowledge and intent can be inferred from objective factual circumstances
The burden is on the employee to prove innocence
Employees are always presumed to know the source
quiz.explanation: Article 4(2) allows intent, knowledge or purpose to be inferred from objective facts. It is not strict liability and there is no reversed burden, but obvious circumstances can establish knowledge.

sessions.title: Risk Assessment, CDD, Beneficial Owners and PEPs
sessions.summary: Apply the Saudi risk-based approach at the front door: the documented risk assessment, when due diligence is required, what must be verified, the 25% beneficial ownership test, simplified and enhanced measures, PEPs and their families, and what to do when due diligence cannot be completed.
objectives: Explain the documented ML/TF risk assessment required by Article 5 of the AML Law and Section 1 of SAMA's Guide
List the five moments when due diligence is required under Article 7/1 of the AML Implementing Regulation
Identify beneficial owners using the 25% test and the control fallbacks, without relying on the customer's word
Apply enhanced measures to high-risk customers and PEPs, and know when simplified measures are allowed

cards.title: A busy morning in Dammam
cards.setting: Customer service hall, Wahat Bank, Al-Faisaliyah branch, Dammam. 9:10 am.

lines.text: Three new customers already this morning: a contracting company, a retired official and a visitor who just wants to send money home.
(on a video call) Perfect timing, Sara. Each one needs a different level of due diligence. Shall we take them one by one?
The contracting company's manager handed me a signed letter naming the owners. Isn't that enough?
SAMA's Guide says we must not rely mainly on the customer's written statement for beneficial ownership. We understand the structure from the records.
And the retired official? He was a deputy minister abroad until last year.
Then he is a foreign PEP. That means senior management approval and questions about source of wealth before we open anything.
Welcome to the Onboarding Hall. Everything here starts from one idea: risk decides how deep we go.

cards.title: The risk-based approach in five scenes

scenes.heading: Know your own risks
scenes.narration: Article 5 of the AML Law requires each bank to identify, assess and document its ML risks, looking at customers, countries, products, services, transactions and delivery channels.

scenes.heading: Keep it current
scenes.narration: SAMA's Guide asks for the assessment to be updated regularly and approved by senior management. New products and technologies must be assessed before launch.

scenes.heading: Rate every customer
scenes.narration: Every customer is classified, for example high, medium or low. A high-risk classification needs senior management approval, based on reasoned information.

scenes.heading: Match effort to risk
scenes.narration: Higher risk means enhanced measures. Lower risk can mean simplified measures, but never when there is a suspicion of money laundering.

scenes.heading: Manage, don't flee
scenes.narration: SAMA's Guide stresses that banks are not banned from high-risk customers. The aim is to control risk, not to exclude whole groups of people.

cards.title: Wahat Bank's risk cycle
cards.caption: SAMA's December 2025 guidance adds a separate business risk assessment covering ML, TF and proliferation financing (see Stage 5).

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Customers, beneficial owners, products, channels and geographies, plus national risk findings.

items.label: Assess and document
items.detail: Written assessment approved by senior management, shared with SAMA on request.

items.label: Set risk appetite
items.detail: Decide which risks the bank will accept before writing controls (Guide 1.2).

items.label: Mitigate
items.detail: Policies, CDD levels, monitoring and limits that match the risk found.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Update regularly, and before new products, technologies or business practices.

cards.question: Under Article 5/5 of the AML Implementing Regulation, when are simplified measures NOT allowed?
options: When the customer is a salaried Saudi national
When there is a suspicion of money laundering
When the account is opened through a digital channel
When the customer has banked with Wahat Bank for years
cards.explanation: Simplified measures are possible for lower risks but are expressly ruled out where money laundering is suspected. Nationality, channel or tenure alone do not decide the question.

cards.title: When due diligence is required (Regulation 7/1)
cards.caption: SAMA's Guide (3.2) adds a sixth trigger: when a customer's transaction does not fit their known behaviour or information.

items.label: New relationship or account
items.detail: Before the relationship starts or the account opens.

items.label: Occasional transaction
items.detail: For a non-customer, whether one transaction or several that appear linked.

items.label: Occasional wire transfer
items.detail: Before a transfer for someone with no established relationship.

items.label: Suspicion of ML
items.detail: Whenever money laundering is suspected, whatever the amount.

items.label: Doubts about data
items.detail: When earlier identification data looks untrue or inadequate.

cards.title: What CDD must cover
cards.body:
Regulation 7/2 and Guide 3.3 set the minimum:

- **Natural person:** full legal name from official documents, residential or national address, date and place of birth, nationality, and (per the Guide) source of income.
- **Legal person:** name, legal form and proof of existence, the powers that bind it, all directors and senior managers, registered address and main place of business, and its sources of revenue.
- **Anyone acting for the customer:** confirm they are authorised and verify their identity.
- **Beneficial owner:** identify and take reasonable steps to verify.
- **Purpose and intended nature** of the relationship, and the ownership and control structure of legal persons.

Verification must use a **reliable, independent source**: never the customer alone, and never the bank's own records. Government-issued data counts as independent. SAMA's Guide (3.9) lets customers update their details without visiting a branch when electronic authentication approved by the National Information Center is used, unless the risk calls for more.

cards.title: Find the beneficial owner of a company
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the order Wahat Bank follows for a corporate customer under Regulation 7/2(c) and Guide 3.18-3.19.
steps: Understand the ownership and control structure from records such as the commercial register and articles of association
Identify any natural person who owns or controls 25% or more of the shares
If nobody reaches 25%, or the controlling holder may not be the real owner, identify who controls the company by other means
As a last resort, identify the natural person holding the senior managing official position
Verify the identities from reliable sources and record the steps and any reasons for doubt

cards.title: Enhanced, standard or simplified?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation into the level of due diligence the Saudi rules point to.

items.text: A former foreign deputy minister opening a private banking account
A customer from a country the AML Permanent Committee lists as high risk
A company with layered holding companies in several jurisdictions
An applicant another bank refused because of suspected ML
A salaried employee opening a current account to receive wages
A small family shop opening a business account with clear ownership
A low-risk payroll product with tight limits and no suspicion
A visitor paying a utility bill at the counter, with no red flags

cards.title: The retired deputy minister
cards.setting: Private banking lounge, Wahat Bank, Riyadh. 2:00 pm.

lines.text: (on the phone) Noura, the retired official wants to deposit SAR 6 million from the sale of a property abroad. He is in a hurry and politely says he 'has nothing to hide'.

Under Regulation 8/5, a foreign PEP needs senior management approval before we establish the relationship, reasonable measures to establish source of wealth and source of funds, and enhanced ongoing monitoring.
His wife and his brother-in-law also want accounts.
Family up to the second degree by blood or marriage count under Regulation 8/3, and SAMA's Guide applies the same enhanced measures to them.
(joining) If he is a good client, I'll approve quickly. But I want the file to show where the wealth came from.
That is exactly the balance the rules expect: we can bank him, with our eyes open.

cards.title: The SAR 6 million deposit
cards.situation: The retired foreign deputy minister offers a sale contract for a villa abroad and a bank letter confirming receipt of the proceeds. He asks Sara to open the account today and says paperwork 'can follow'. His brother-in-law, a local businessman, wants a separate account to receive part of the funds.

choices.text: Open both accounts today and complete PEP checks within the month
choices.outcome: Regulation 8/5 requires senior management approval before establishing the relationship with a foreign PEP. Opening first and checking later breaks that order.

choices.text: Decline both because foreign PEPs are too risky for Wahat Bank
choices.outcome: The Guide does not ask banks to avoid whole groups of customers. Refusing may be possible under risk appetite, but blanket refusal is not the expected response.

choices.text: Verify the sale documents, assess source of wealth and funds, obtain senior management approval, then open with enhanced monitoring; treat the brother-in-law as a family member under the same measures
choices.outcome: Best choice. This follows Regulation 8/5 and Guide 4.13-4.14: approval first, source of wealth and funds established, enhanced ongoing monitoring, and the same measures for family and close associates.

choices.text: Open the account for the brother-in-law only, because he is not a PEP himself
choices.outcome: A relative by marriage within the second degree is a family member of the PEP under Regulation 8/3, so he cannot be treated as an ordinary customer, and routing funds through him is a classic concealment pattern.

cards.title: PEP measures in Saudi Arabia
cards.caption: Family members (up to second degree) and close associates receive the same treatment. A decision that a domestic PEP is not high risk needs documented grounds.

cards.back: Someone entrusted with a prominent public function in the Kingdom or abroad, or a senior position in an international organisation.
Anyone related to the PEP by blood or marriage up to the second degree (Regulation 8/3).
Someone with joint beneficial ownership or a close business relationship with the PEP, or who owns an entity set up for the PEP's benefit.
How the customer built their overall fortune over time.
Where the specific money used in the relationship or transaction comes from.
If another institution refused the customer, Guide 4.5 asks you to apply EDD and find out why.

cards.question: A company's manager gives Sara a signed letter naming its owners. What does SAMA's Guide (3.19) say?
options: Accept it, since the manager signed it
Do not rely mainly on it; understand the structure from records
Accept it if a notary has stamped it
Ask the owners to sign a second letter
cards.explanation: Guide 3.19 says the institution should not rely primarily on the customer's written statement and should understand the ownership and control structure using records such as the commercial register, shareholder register and articles of association.

cards.title: When you cannot finish CDD
cards.body:
- **Cannot complete due diligence?** Regulation 7/8: do not open the account, start the relationship or carry out the transaction. For an existing customer, end the relationship. In every case, consider a suspicious transaction report.
- **Worried that CDD questions will tip off a suspect?** Regulation 7/9 and Guide 8.7 let the bank stop the CDD and file a report to the FIU instead, stating why CDD was not done.
- **Occasional customers:** Guide 5.8 limits exchange, transfers and cheque cashing for non-customers to SAR 5,000 per transaction and SAR 50,000 a year.
- **No anonymous, numbered or fictitious-name accounts** (AML Law Article 6).

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Risk drives everything: a documented, senior-approved risk assessment and a risk rating for every customer.
Due diligence is needed at five moments in Regulation 7/1, and SAMA adds behaviour that does not fit the customer.
Beneficial owners: 25% ownership, then control by other means, then the senior managing official, verified from records, not the customer's letter.
Foreign PEPs are always high risk: senior approval first, source of wealth and funds, enhanced monitoring; family to the second degree too.
If CDD cannot be completed, do not proceed, and consider reporting; if CDD would tip off a suspect, report instead.

cards.prompt: Which part of the onboarding process in your team is most likely to be rushed under customer pressure? What would you say to a valued customer who wants the account opened before the checks are done?

quiz.question: Which list correctly states three of the five due diligence triggers in Regulation 7/1 of the AML Implementing Regulation?
options: Any cash deposit, any transfer, any cheque
Suspicion of ML, salary increase, change of address
New relationship, suspicion of ML, doubts about earlier data
New relationship, annual review, change of branch
quiz.explanation: Regulation 7/1 lists a new relationship or account, occasional transactions, occasional wire transfers, suspicion of ML and doubts about earlier data. Annual reviews or a change of branch are not on that list.

quiz.question: Under Regulation 7/2(c), which natural person must a bank first look for when identifying the beneficial owner of a company?
options: Anyone owning at least 10% of the shares
The person who signs the account application
The largest corporate shareholder
Anyone owning or controlling 25% or more of the shares
quiz.explanation: The first test is a natural person owning or controlling 25% or more. If none exists or there is doubt, the bank looks to control by other means and, last, to the senior managing official. A corporate shareholder is never the end point.

quiz.question: A customer is a former foreign minister. Under Regulation 8/5, which measure is required before the relationship is established?
options: Approval from senior management
A guarantee from his embassy
A notification to the FIU
Approval from SAMA
quiz.explanation: For foreign PEPs the bank needs senior management approval, reasonable measures on source of wealth and funds, and enhanced monitoring. No SAMA approval or FIU notification is required simply because of PEP status.

quiz.question: How far does the definition of a PEP's family member reach under Regulation 8/3?
options: Relatives by blood only, up to the third degree
Relatives by blood or marriage up to the second degree
Anyone living in the same household
Spouse and children only
quiz.explanation: Regulation 8/3 covers relatives by blood or marriage up to the second degree, so in-laws such as a brother-in-law can be included.

quiz.question: A new account holder's details cannot be verified because his documents conflict and he refuses to explain. What does Regulation 7/8 require?
options: Refer him to another branch for a second try
Do not open the account and consider filing a suspicious transaction report
Open it with a low limit until he explains
Open it and verify within ninety days
quiz.explanation: If due diligence cannot be completed, the bank must not open the account, establish the relationship or carry out the transaction, and must consider reporting to the FIU.

quiz.question: An occasional customer with no account asks to cash cheques. Under SAMA Guide 5.8, what limits apply to cheque cashing, transfers and exchange for occasional customers?
options: SAR 5,000 per transaction and SAR 50,000 a year
SAR 60,000 per transaction and SAR 500,000 a year
SAR 3,000 per transaction with no annual limit
SAR 10,000 per transaction and SAR 100,000 a year
quiz.explanation: Guide 5.8 allows occasional customers to exchange currency, transfer money and cash cheques up to SAR 5,000 per transaction and no more than SAR 50,000 (or equivalents) in one year.

quiz.question: Sara suspects a would-be customer is laundering money, and believes that asking detailed CDD questions will alert him. What do Regulation 7/9 and Guide 8.7 allow?
options: Complete full CDD anyway and decide on a report later
Open the account so that monitoring can gather evidence
Stop the CDD and file a report to the FIU explaining why
Ask him to come back with a family member
quiz.explanation: Where suspicion exists and CDD may tip off the customer, the bank may choose not to carry out CDD and must file a suspicious transaction report stating why CDD was not applied.

quiz.question: Wahat Bank's compliance team rates a customer as high risk. Under SAMA Guide 1.9, what must happen?
options: The account is closed after twelve months
The customer is told and may appeal the rating
SAMA approves the classification within five days
Senior management approves the classification, based on reasoned information
quiz.explanation: Guide 1.9 requires senior management approval of a high-risk classification, supported by acceptable and reasoned information. There is no SAMA approval step and no duty to inform the customer.

quiz.question: Wahat Bank plans to launch a new instant cross-border transfer app. When must it assess the ML/TF risks of the new product?
options: Before launching it
Only if SAMA asks for it
Within a year of launch
After the first suspicious report
quiz.explanation: Article 5 of the AML Law, Regulation 5/6 and Guide 1.7 require risks from new products, practices and technologies to be assessed before launch or first use.

quiz.question: A domestic PEP's relationship manager wants to rate him as standard risk. What does SAMA Guide 4.16 require?
options: Approval from the Saudi FIU
Nothing, since domestic PEPs are always low risk
Sufficient, documented grounds based on the risk assessment
Written consent from the PEP himself
quiz.explanation: Domestic PEPs are not automatically high risk, but Guide 4.16 requires sufficient, reasonable and documented grounds, based on the risk assessment, for deciding that a local PEP, their family or associates are not high risk.

sessions.title: Monitoring, Suspicious Transaction Reporting and Tipping Off
sessions.summary: Learn how Saudi banks monitor accounts, escalate unusual activity, report to the Saudi FIU promptly and regardless of amount, protect the confidentiality of reports, keep records for ten years and respond to requests from the FIU and the Public Prosecution.
objectives: Explain the monitoring duties in Article 13 of the AML Law and SAMA's expectation of electronic monitoring systems
Follow the internal escalation and reporting route to the Saudi FIU under Articles 15 and 70 and Section 8 of SAMA's Guide
Apply the tipping-off ban and the good-faith protection in Articles 16 and 71
State the ten-year record-keeping rule and how to respond to FIU and Public Prosecution requests

cards.title: A pattern on the screen
cards.setting: Transaction monitoring room, Wahat Bank head office, Riyadh. 10:05 am.

lines.text: Noura, look at this. A dental clinic account in Jeddah: forty cash deposits of just under SAR 50,000 over three weeks, then transfers to three trading firms in different countries.
Does the clinic's turnover explain it?
Its CDD file says monthly revenue of about SAR 200,000. This is ten times that.
(joining from Jeddah) The owner's brother came in yesterday asking why one transfer was delayed. My teller nearly told him that compliance was looking at it.
Nearly is the important word. Let's walk through what the law expects from each of us, from the teller to the person who files the report.
Welcome to the Signal Room. Our job is to notice, escalate, report and stay silent.

cards.title: From alert to report in six scenes

scenes.heading: Monitor
scenes.narration: Article 13 of the AML Law requires ongoing scrutiny of transactions so they match what the bank knows about the customer, their business, risk profile and, where needed, source of funds.

scenes.heading: Examine
scenes.narration: Complex, unusually large transactions and unusual patterns with no clear economic or legal purpose must be examined, with closer monitoring for higher-risk customers.

scenes.heading: Escalate
scenes.narration: Staff raise concerns through the internal channel to the officer responsible for reporting. SAMA's Guide asks for board-approved reporting procedures.

scenes.heading: Investigate
scenes.narration: The AML/CTF unit investigates, with set levels of review and approval, and documents every decision, including decisions not to report.

scenes.heading: Report
scenes.narration: If there are reasonable grounds to suspect, the bank reports promptly and directly to the Saudi FIU, whatever the amount, and includes attempted transactions.

scenes.heading: Stay silent
scenes.narration: Nobody may tell the customer or anyone else that a report is planned, made or under investigation. Good-faith reporters are protected from liability.

cards.title: Escalate or explainable?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each observation should be escalated to the AML/CTF unit or is explained by what the bank knows.

items.text: Repeated cash deposits just below an internal review level, with no business reason
A customer cancels a transfer when asked about its purpose
A student account suddenly receives large transfers from many unrelated people
Funds arrive and leave within a day through several countries
A monthly salary credit followed by normal bill payments
A seasonal rise in a retailer's takings during Ramadan, in line with past years
A documented home sale followed by a payment to the buyer's lender
A company with a sudden spike in trade payments to a high-risk country, unlike its history

cards.question: The jeweller's account shows an attempted SAR 300,000 transfer that the customer cancelled when asked for documents. Does SAMA's Guide expect a report?
options: No, because the money never left the bank
Yes, if there are reasonable grounds for suspicion, even though it was only attempted
Only if the amount is above SAR 500,000
cards.explanation: Article 15 of the AML Law and Guide 8.4 require reports on suspicious transactions including unsuccessful attempts, regardless of value, where there are reasonable grounds to suspect.

cards.title: What SAMA expects in a report
cards.body:
**Reasonable grounds, not speculation.** Guide 8.6 says reports should not be based on guesswork or lack of information; they rest on what the bank knows or on sufficient information linking the activity to suspicion.

**Minimum content (Regulation 15/4):** names, addresses and phone numbers of those involved; a description of the transaction, the parties, how it was detected and its status; the amount and accounts; and the reasons for suspicion. The FIU's own form and channel are used (Guide 8.8).

**Supporting technical report (Guide 8.9):** an account statement for **six months**, the CDD documents, and a technical analysis of the account or contract.

**Decisions not to report (Guide 8.10):** the reporting officer documents the reasons in detail, with the required review and approval levels.

**Records (Guide 8.11 and 6.7):** copies of reports to the FIU and of internal reports that were closed are kept confidentially for at least ten years, with named people allowed access.

cards.title: The Wahat Bank reporting route
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the order Wahat Bank's board-approved procedure follows.
steps: A front-line employee notices unusual activity and records the facts
The employee raises an internal report through the channel to the reporting officer
The AML/CTF unit investigates, reviewing CDD, transactions and context
The case goes through the set review and approval levels
If there are reasonable grounds, the reporting officer files the report with the Saudi FIU on its form
The bank sends the technical report and answers any FIU request for further information promptly

lines.text: The clinic owner's brother is back. He says the family will move all its accounts unless someone explains the delay right now.
(on the phone) What has the teller said so far?
Only that the transfer is 'being processed'. He wants to know if there is 'a problem with the authorities'.

Article 16 of the AML Law and Article 71 of the CTF Law forbid disclosing that a report will be, is being or has been made, or that an investigation is under way. That applies to you, the teller, me and the board.
But I can't lie to him either.
You don't need to. Say you can't discuss internal reviews, offer to take his contact details, and pass any new information to us. Let's look at the options.

cards.title: Tipping off at the counter
cards.situation: The clinic owner's brother demands to know whether 'the government' is looking at the family's money. He is not the account holder but says he manages the clinic's finances. He threatens to close all accounts and complain to SAMA if nobody explains the held transfer.

choices.text: Tell him quietly that compliance has flagged the account, so he understands it is not the branch's fault
choices.outcome: This is tipping off. Revealing that the account has been flagged breaches Article 16 and could alert the suspects. Good intentions do not change that.

choices.text: Explain that the bank cannot discuss internal reviews or third-party accounts, note his concerns and contact details, and inform the AML/CTF unit straight away
choices.outcome: Best choice. It is truthful, discloses nothing about a report, respects customer confidentiality and gives the AML/CTF unit useful information.

choices.text: Release the transfer to calm him down and avoid a complaint
choices.outcome: Releasing funds to avoid a confrontation can facilitate laundering and undermine the FIU's analysis. Decisions on the transaction belong to the AML/CTF unit.

choices.text: Refuse to speak to him and ask security to escort him out
choices.outcome: This avoids tipping off but escalates the situation and loses the chance to record useful information. A calm, scripted response is better.

cards.title: Allowed and not allowed under the tipping-off ban
cards.caption: Articles 16 and 71 protect the confidentiality of reports and investigations while allowing the communications the bank needs to work.

items.label: Telling the customer a report was filed
Discussing the case with colleagues who need to know
Asking the bank's lawyers for advice

cards.back: Staff and directors who report suspicions in good faith are protected from criminal, civil, contractual, disciplinary and administrative liability (Regulation 16/1).

cards.front: Even if the crime is unclear
cards.back: Protection applies even if the reporter did not know the exact crime, and whether or not a crime actually happened.
The FIU may stop a suspicious transaction for up to 72 hours from receiving the report (Regulation 17/1(q)).
If the request relates to the bank's own report, the FIU asks the bank directly; otherwise it asks through SAMA (Regulation 18/1).
The Public Prosecution may order seizure for up to 60 days, without prior notice; a court can extend it (Article 44).
Knowing of an attempt to commit or finance a terrorist crime and not reporting it, when able to, can mean up to five years in prison (CTF Law Article 54).

cards.question: Under Article 12 of the AML Law, how long must CDD records and account files be kept?
options: At least five years after the account closes
At least ten years after the relationship ends
Until the customer asks for deletion
For as long as SAMA's inspection cycle lasts
cards.explanation: Article 12 requires transaction records and CDD records to be kept for at least ten years from the transaction or the end of the relationship. The Public Prosecution may require a longer period in specific cases.

cards.title: Numbers to remember in the Signal Room

items.label: Minimum record retention
items.detail: Transactions, CDD files, reports and investigations (Art. 12, Guide 6.1, 6.7).

items.label: FIU stop power
items.detail: Maximum period the FIU may stop a suspicious transaction (Reg. 17/1(q)).

items.label: Statement in the technical report
items.detail: Account statement period sent to the FIU with a report (Guide 8.9).

items.label: Provisional seizure
items.detail: Maximum Public Prosecution seizure without a court extension (Art. 44).

items.label: Reporting threshold
items.detail: There is none: reports are due whatever the amount (Art. 15, Reg. 15/2).

cards.title: Monitoring is people plus systems
cards.body:
- SAMA's Guide (7.5) and Account Opening Rule 8 say **manual monitoring alone is not enough**: banks need electronic systems integrated with core banking and linked to customer risk ratings.
- But Guide 7.8 also says the bank must **train staff** and not rely only on systems. Your judgment at the counter still matters.
- Monitoring tools must be **tested at least once a year** (Guide 7.6) and indicators updated using internal cases and FIU feedback (Guide 8.12).
- **Wire transfers:** if required originator or beneficiary information is missing, the transfer must not be executed (AML Law Article 10).

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Monitor every customer against what you know about them; examine complex, large or unusual activity with no clear purpose.
Escalate internally first; the bank reports to the Saudi FIU promptly and directly, whatever the amount, including attempts.
Reports need reasonable grounds, a supporting technical report with six months of statements, and documented reasons when a case is closed without a report.
Never tip off: no hints to the customer or anyone else. Internal, legal and official communications are allowed, and good-faith reporters are protected.
Keep records for at least ten years, and answer FIU and Public Prosecution requests accurately and without disclosure.

cards.prompt: Imagine a customer asks you directly whether 'something is wrong' with their account. Write down the exact words you would use to stay truthful without tipping them off.

quiz.question: What reporting threshold applies to suspicious transaction reports under Article 15 of the AML Law and Regulation 15/2?
options: Any amount above the customer's declared income
None: the duty applies regardless of the amount
SAR 50,000 per transaction or linked series
SAR 100,000 in a single month
quiz.explanation: Article 15 and Regulation 15/2 make the reporting duty apply whatever the amount involved. There is no monetary threshold for suspicion.

quiz.question: Which of these may a Wahat Bank employee lawfully do after an internal report has been made?
options: Let the customer know so they can explain themselves
Warn a friend at another bank about the customer
Hint to the customer's relative that the authorities are interested
Discuss the case with the bank's lawyers for advice
quiz.explanation: Article 16 allows communications between directors and employees and with lawyers or competent authorities. Disclosing to the customer, relatives or outsiders is prohibited.

quiz.question: How long may the Saudi FIU stop a suspicious transaction after receiving a report, under Regulation 17/1(q)?
options: Up to 72 hours
Up to 30 days
Until a court rules
Up to 24 hours
quiz.explanation: The implementing regulation lets the Directorate stop a suspicious transaction, if necessary, for up to 72 hours from receipt of the report. Longer restraint needs the Public Prosecution's seizure power.

quiz.question: Which documents does SAMA Guide 8.9 expect in the technical report sent to the FIU?
options: A signed statement from the customer explaining the activity
The customer's tax returns for three years and a credit report
A six-month account statement, CDD documents and a technical analysis
The teller's personnel file and branch CCTV footage
quiz.explanation: Guide 8.9 lists an account statement or contract transactions for six months, the CDD documents and a technical report examining the account. Asking the customer for a statement could tip them off.

quiz.question: The AML/CTF unit investigates an internal report and decides not to report to the FIU. What does SAMA Guide 8.10 require?
options: Detailed documentation of the reasons, with the set review levels
Asking SAMA to confirm the decision in writing
Telling the employee who raised it to drop the matter
Deleting the internal report to protect the customer
quiz.explanation: Guide 8.10 requires the reporting officer to document the reasons for not reporting in sufficient detail, following the approval and review levels. Guide 8.11 requires those internal reports to be kept.

quiz.question: A teller reports a suspicion in good faith. The FIU later finds no crime occurred. Is the teller exposed to disciplinary action for the report?
options: Yes, if the customer complains about the report
Only if the bank's lawyers approved the report
Yes, unless the teller named the exact predicate crime
No: good-faith reporters are protected even if no crime occurred
quiz.explanation: Regulation 16/1 extends the protection to criminal, civil, contractual, disciplinary and administrative liability, even when the reporter did not know the exact crime and whether or not illegal activity actually occurred.

quiz.question: The FIU contacts Wahat Bank asking for information about a customer the bank has never reported. Under Regulation 18/1, how should the request reach the bank?
options: Through the Anti-Money Laundering Permanent Committee
Through SAMA, as the supervisory authority
Directly by phone to the branch manager
Through the customer's lawyer
quiz.explanation: The FIU may request information directly only when it relates to a report the bank filed. In other cases the request goes through the supervisory authority, SAMA.

quiz.question: A wire transfer arrives at Wahat Bank's payments team for onward sending, but the required originator information is missing and cannot be obtained. What does Article 10 of the AML Law require of the ordering institution in this situation?
options: Execute it if the amount is small
Execute it and ask for the data within a month
Not to execute the wire transfer
Execute it and report it to SAMA at quarter end
quiz.explanation: Article 10 says an institution unable to obtain the required originator or beneficiary information must not permit the transfer. Receiving and intermediary banks also need risk-based procedures for transfers missing information.

quiz.question: Under Article 54 of the CTF Law, what can happen to someone who knew of an attempt to finance a terrorist crime and, though able to, did not report it?
options: A prison term of up to five years
No penalty, as reporting is voluntary
A fine of up to SAR 10,000
Only a written warning from SAMA
quiz.explanation: Article 54 sets a prison term of up to five years for failing to report a known attempt to commit or finance a terrorist crime when able to do so.

quiz.question: Why does SAMA's Guide (7.5) say Wahat Bank cannot rely on staff checking statements by hand?
options: SAMA bans staff from reviewing customer statements
Manual checks breach customer data protection rules
Electronic systems remove the need for trained staff
Manual monitoring alone is not sufficient; electronic systems are needed
quiz.explanation: Guide 7.5 and Account Opening Rule 8 require effective electronic monitoring integrated with core systems. Guide 7.8 still requires trained staff, so systems complement people rather than replace them.

sessions.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions and Proliferation Financing
sessions.summary: Apply SAMA's December 2025 Rules for the Implementation of Targeted Financial Sanctions: what to screen and when, how to handle alerts with maker-checker review, freezing without delay and without prior notice, notifying SAMA, lifting freezes, confidentiality, records, role-based training, and how proliferation financing fits in.
objectives: Explain which UN Security Council regimes the TFS Rules implement and what 'without delay' means
Describe who and what must be screened, and the six screening moments in the TFS Rules
Handle a screening alert from review to freeze, notification to SAMA and record keeping
Recognise sanctions evasion and proliferation financing risks and know when a report goes to the FIU

cards.title: A new name at midnight
cards.setting: Sanctions unit, Wahat Bank head office, Riyadh. 7:45 am.

lines.text: Noura, the UN Security Council added several names overnight. The official channels published the update at 11 pm and our list loaded at 6 am.
Seven hours. The TFS Rules define 'without delay' as within hours of a listing. Did the overnight batch screen against the new names?
Yes, and we have one strong match: a trading company customer whose 60% owner looks like a newly listed individual.
Then this is a test of everything SAMA asked for in December 2025: screening, alert handling, freezing and confidentiality.
(joining) Shouldn't legal and the executive committee approve before we freeze a big corporate client?
No, and the Rules say so explicitly. Let's open the Freeze Vault and I'll show you why.

cards.title: SAMA's TFS Rules in six scenes

scenes.heading: What they implement
scenes.narration: The Rules apply UN Security Council measures against terrorism and its financing, including resolutions 1267, 1989, 2253, 1988 and 1373, and against proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, including 1718 and 1737.

scenes.heading: Without delay
scenes.narration: SAMA defines 'without delay' as within hours of a person being listed or delisted. Freezing does not wait for committees, legal reviews or management sign-off once a match is confirmed.

scenes.heading: Governance
scenes.narration: Each bank needs a sanctions compliance programme, a specialised TFS unit linked to the AML/CTF unit, a competent officer, board-approved policies and an annual independent test.

scenes.heading: Screening
scenes.narration: Customers, beneficial owners, directors, authorised signatories and related parties such as correspondent banks and remittance beneficiaries are all screened, at set moments.

scenes.heading: Freeze and notify
scenes.narration: Funds of listed persons, and of those they own, control or act for, are frozen without prior notice. The bank then notifies SAMA through its dedicated sanctions channel.

scenes.heading: Train for it
scenes.narration: Chapter Eight requires risk-based, role-tailored training: simulations for specialists, in-person workshops for the sanctions unit, e-learning for others and focused awareness for the board.

cards.title: When Wahat Bank must screen (TFS Rules 3.5-3.6)
cards.caption: After a new listing, the bank also reviews its transactions from the previous twelve months for past dealings with the listed person (3.4).

items.label: Before onboarding
items.detail: Before a new relationship, account, wallet or remittance membership.

items.label: Before any transaction
items.detail: Outgoing items before execution; incoming items as soon as received.

items.label: On every list update
items.detail: Screen the whole database against the update and record the result.

items.label: On data updates
items.detail: Whenever customer information is updated or reviewed.

items.label: Every quarter
items.detail: Comprehensive screening at least once every three months.

items.label: On trigger events
items.detail: Ownership changes, new high-risk countries, risk upgrades, adverse media.

cards.question: What does 'without delay' mean in SAMA's Rules for the Implementation of Targeted Financial Sanctions?
options: Within five business days of a listing
By the end of the next working day
Within hours of a listing or delisting
As soon as the board has approved
cards.explanation: The Rules define 'without delay' as within hours of a designation or delisting. Paragraph 5.5 adds that freezing must not wait for internal committees, legal review or senior management approval once a match is confirmed.

cards.title: Must Wahat Bank screen this party?
cards.prompt: Decide which parties the TFS Rules (3.1 and 3.4) require the bank to screen against the sanctions lists.

items.text: The customer's beneficial owner
A director of a corporate customer
An authorised signatory acting for the customer
A correspondent bank in the payment chain
The beneficiary of an outgoing remittance
An intermediary in a trade transaction
A competitor bank that is not part of the transaction
A customer's neighbour with no link to the account

cards.title: Alert handling under Chapter Five
cards.body:
**Two specialists (maker-checker).** Every alert is reviewed by two people with enough TFS knowledge, using CDD data, public records and open sources (5.3).

**False match?** The specialists may close it after following the procedure, keeping a **written justification** (5.4). Repeated false matches may go on an internal 'whitelist', but that list needs board or senior management approval, periodic review and is still screened (5.8).

**Cannot close it?** Escalate straight to a senior manager with the right expertise. If there are sufficient grounds of a direct or indirect link to a listed person, **freeze without delay**, with no wait for committees, legal review or management approval (5.5).

**Document everything (5.6):** time received, time processed and escalated, list source, type of match, action and reasons, names of the specialists, outcome and freeze details.

**Confidentiality (5.7):** never reveal a match, an intended freeze or an ongoing review to the customer or anyone else, except reports to SAMA and the FIU.

lines.text: Maker-checker is done. Date of birth, nationality and passport number match the listing. My checker agrees: true match.
The listed individual owns 60% of the trading company. The company itself is not named on the list.
So we only freeze his personal account? The company has payroll due tomorrow for 200 workers.
Paragraph 6.6 is clear: entities owned or controlled by a listed person are covered even if they are not named. The company's funds are frozen too.
And the payroll?
We freeze now and notify SAMA. We never release frozen funds on our own initiative; any question about them is raised with SAMA.

cards.title: Freeze the company too?
cards.situation: Wahat Bank confirms that a newly listed individual owns 60% of a corporate customer. The company's general manager, who is not listed, calls to ask why a supplier payment has not gone through. The executive committee meets tomorrow, and the corporate banking head suggests waiting for its view because the client is profitable.

choices.text: Wait for tomorrow's executive committee before acting on the company's accounts
choices.outcome: Paragraph 5.5 forbids delaying a freeze for committee, legal or management approval once a match is confirmed. A day's wait could let funds leave.

choices.text: Freeze the individual's and the company's funds now, without prior notice, block new services, notify SAMA, and tell the manager only that the payment cannot be processed at present
choices.outcome: Best choice. The freeze covers entities owned or controlled by the listed person (6.1, 6.6), must be immediate and unannounced, must be notified to SAMA (5.9), and nothing is disclosed about the match (5.7).

choices.text: Freeze only the individual's personal account, because the company is not named on the list
choices.outcome: The Rules extend freezing to funds owned or controlled directly or indirectly by the listed person, including companies not formally named (6.3, 6.6).

choices.text: Freeze both accounts and explain to the manager that his owner has been listed by the UN
choices.outcome: Freezing is right, but explaining the match to the manager breaches the confidentiality required by paragraphs 5.7 and 9.2. Public listings exist, but the bank must not disclose its own match or actions.

cards.title: Freezing and lifting a freeze
cards.caption: Joint funds with a non-listed person are frozen in full; the non-listed share may be dealt with only after consulting SAMA (6.4).

items.label: Trigger
items.left: Confirmed match with a listed person
items.right: Delisting by the UN sanctions committee

items.label: Scope
items.left: Owned, controlled or agent funds, joint accounts

items.label: Exception
items.left: Pre-freeze contract earnings credited but frozen
items.right: Not if a 1373 instruction or SAMA says otherwise

cards.back: A natural or legal person, group or organisation on a sanctions list issued under the UN mechanisms.
A party that is not itself listed but is owned, controlled by or acting for a listed person.
Attempts to get round sanctions, for example through front companies, relatives or complex structures; if suspected, a report goes to the FIU (5.10).
Names confirmed as repeated false matches, excluded from alerts only with approval, review and continued screening.
After a new listing, transactions of the previous twelve months are reviewed for past dealings (3.4).
Systems must catch aliases, spelling variants, similar-sounding names and transliterations (3.7).

cards.title: Where does each action go?
cards.prompt: Match each situation to the right recipient or action under SAMA's rules.

pairs.left: Funds frozen after a confirmed match
pairs.right: Notify SAMA through its dedicated sanctions channel with the freeze details

pairs.left: Signs of an attempt to evade sanctions
pairs.right: Submit a suspicious activity report to the Saudi FIU

pairs.left: Funds of a listed person held elsewhere that you discover
pairs.right: Notify SAMA in writing with the details

pairs.left: Freeze lifted after a UN delisting

pairs.right: Update internal lists immediately and screen all data

cards.question: A listed person and his non-listed wife hold a joint savings account. What do the TFS Rules (6.4) require?
options: Freeze only the husband's half
Freeze the whole account; the wife's share is released only after consulting SAMA
Leave the account open because the wife is not listed
Close the account and pay the balance to the wife
cards.explanation: Paragraph 6.4 extends the freeze to funds held jointly with a non-listed person, including that person's share, which may only be dealt with after consulting SAMA.

cards.title: Proliferation financing in the risk cycle
cards.caption: SAMA's December 2025 business risk guidance requires the assessment to distinguish clearly between ML, TF and PF risks.

items.label: Assess PF risk
items.detail: Identify, assess and document PF risk separately from ML and TF (TFS 2.1, 2025 guidance).

items.label: Screen for PF regimes
items.detail: Include UN lists on weapons of mass destruction, such as those under resolutions 1718 and 1737.

items.label: Watch trade and payments
items.detail: Look for evasion through intermediaries, front companies and complex ownership.

items.label: Freeze and notify
items.detail: Apply the same freeze-without-delay rules and notify SAMA.

items.label: Learn and update
items.detail: Feed cases into indicators, training and the business risk assessment.

cards.title: Seven habits of a good sanctions screener
cards.body:
- Check the official sources: the PCTC site under the Presidency of State Security, the MOFA site for Chapter VII resolutions and the UN committees (9.6, 9.7).
- Record when each list update arrived and when it went live (4.1).
- Never close an alert without a written reason.
- Look beyond names: ownership, control and agents.
- Never delay a confirmed freeze for sign-offs.
- Say nothing outside official channels.
- Keep TFS records for at least **ten years** (7.3), including the record of training given.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: SAMA's December 2025 TFS Rules apply UN counter-terrorism and counter-proliferation sanctions; 'without delay' means within hours.
Screen customers, beneficial owners, directors, signatories and related parties at onboarding, before every transaction, on every list update, on data updates, quarterly and on trigger events.
Alerts get maker-checker review; false matches need a written reason; confirmed matches are frozen at once, with no wait for approvals.
Freezing covers owned, controlled and joint funds, without prior notice; notify SAMA after freezing and after lifting a freeze, and report evasion to the FIU.
Confidentiality, ten-year records and role-based training with simulations are part of the Rules, not extras.

cards.prompt: Where in your role could a sanctioned person reach Wahat Bank indirectly: through an owner, a signatory, a beneficiary or an intermediary? What would you check first?

quiz.question: Which UN Security Council resolutions do SAMA's TFS Rules name for proliferation of weapons of mass destruction?
options: Resolutions 1718 and 1737 and later related resolutions
Resolutions 2253 and 1988 only
Resolution 1373 only
Resolutions 1267 and 1989 only
quiz.explanation: The Rules list 1267, 1989, 2253, 1988 and 1373 for terrorism and its financing, and 1718 and 1737 for proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and its financing.

quiz.question: How often must Wahat Bank run a comprehensive screening of its whole customer base under TFS Rule 3.6(b)?
options: Only when SAMA requests it
At least once every three months
At least once every six months
At least once a year
quiz.explanation: Rule 3.6(b) requires comprehensive screening of customer data, transactions, beneficial owners, directors, signatories and related parties at least once every three months, on top of screening at onboarding, before transactions and after list updates.

quiz.question: An incoming international transfer arrives at 10 am. When must it be screened under TFS Rule 3.6(a)?
options: Only if the amount is large
Within three working days
As soon as it is received
At the end-of-day batch run
quiz.explanation: Outgoing transactions are screened before execution and incoming ones as soon as they are received, without waiting for the end of the day or another period.

quiz.question: Who must review a sanctions screening alert under TFS Rule 5.3?
options: The external auditor
The customer's relationship manager alone
Any branch employee on duty
Two specialists with TFS knowledge, as maker and checker
quiz.explanation: Rule 5.3 requires dual review by two specialists with sufficient TFS experience and knowledge. A relationship manager alone would lack independence and specialist knowledge.

quiz.question: A screening specialist confirms a true match on a customer late on a Thursday. The legal department is closed until Sunday. What does TFS Rule 5.5 require?
options: Freeze only if senior management agrees on Sunday
Freeze the funds without delay, without waiting for legal review
Ask the customer to explain before freezing
Wait for the legal department's opinion on Sunday
quiz.explanation: Rule 5.5 says freezing must not be delayed pending an internal committee, legal review, senior management approval or any other reason once the match is confirmed.

quiz.question: After freezing funds, whom must Wahat Bank notify under TFS Rule 5.9?
options: The bank's external auditor
The customer, in writing
SAMA, through its dedicated sanctions email channel
The Capital Market Authority
quiz.explanation: Rule 5.9 requires notification to SAMA after the freeze, with customer and transaction details, the nature and value of the funds and the listing information. The customer is not notified in advance.

quiz.question: A company is not on any sanctions list, but a newly listed individual controls it through his minor son's shareholding. What do the TFS Rules require?
options: Do nothing, since the company is not named
Close the account and return the funds
Freeze only if the son is also listed
Freeze the company's funds, as it is controlled by a listed person
quiz.explanation: Rules 6.3 and 6.6 extend the freeze to entities owned or controlled by a listed person, including through minor children or spouses, even if not named on the list.

quiz.question: The UN delists a person whose funds Wahat Bank froze. No instruction under resolution 1373 or from SAMA says otherwise. What should the bank do?
options: Lift the freeze without delay and notify SAMA immediately
Ask the customer to apply to a court
Lift it after the next quarterly screening
Keep the freeze for twelve months as a precaution
quiz.explanation: Rule 6.9 requires the freeze to be lifted without delay and without prior notice on delisting, unless instructed otherwise; Rule 6.10 requires immediate written notification to SAMA.

quiz.question: The sanctions team sees a customer routing payments through a chain of new front companies after a relative was listed. No listed name appears. What does TFS Rule 5.10 require if there are signs of evasion?
options: Wait for the quarterly screening
Submit a suspicious activity report to the Saudi FIU
Close the case because no listed name matched
Notify the customer's other banks
quiz.explanation: Rule 5.10 requires checks for circumvention through ownership structures, intermediaries and transaction patterns, and a suspicious activity report to the FIU where there are indications of evasion.

quiz.question: How long must TFS records, including alerts, freezes and training records, be kept under TFS Rule 7.3?
options: Until the listed person is delisted
Three years after the next SAMA inspection
At least five years from the alert date
At least ten years from completing the transaction or procedure
quiz.explanation: Rule 7.3 sets a minimum of ten years from the completion of the transaction or procedure; Rule 7.1(k) includes a statement of training and awareness activities.

sessions.title: The Bank's Programme: Governance, Training, Audit and Penalties
sessions.summary: Prepare for SAMA's review: the business risk assessment under the December 2025 guidance, the AML/CTF compliance function, independent audit, staff screening, the training duties in Section 11 of SAMA's Guide, record keeping, and the supervisory and criminal penalties for failure, illustrated by SAMA's own enforcement announcements.
objectives: Describe the six stages of a business risk assessment and the difference between inherent and residual risk
Explain the role, independence and duties of the AML/CTF compliance officer and the independent audit function
Apply SAMA's training requirements: who is trained, when, how deeply, how knowledge is tested and what is recorded
Summarise SAMA's supervisory measures, the criminal penalties in the AML and CTF Laws, and what SAMA's enforcement announcements show

cards.title: Two weeks to the review
cards.setting: Board meeting room, Wahat Bank head office, Riyadh. 4:00 pm.

lines.text: SAMA's review team arrives in two weeks. I want a straight answer: are we ready?
Mostly. Our business risk assessment needs updating to the December 2025 guidance, which asks for ML, TF and proliferation financing to be assessed separately.
And the sanctions unit's simulation exercises are done, but I still need to document the comprehension test results for senior management.
Two of my new tellers started before their AML course was recorded in the system. The course happened, but the record is missing.
Then we fix the record honestly and check why it happened. Section 11.5 of SAMA's Guide expects training documents, attendance and dates to be kept.
Good. Walk me through what SAMA will look for, and what happens to banks that fail.

cards.title: What SAMA looks for in six scenes

scenes.heading: A real risk assessment
scenes.narration: A written business risk assessment built for the bank itself, separating ML, TF and PF risk, approved by the board or senior management and updated at least once a year.

scenes.heading: A senior, independent officer
scenes.narration: An AML/CTF compliance officer at senior management level who works independently, reports to the board and its committees, and can see any data needed.

scenes.heading: Independent testing
